19912-the-insurrection-in-paris:
The Insurrection in Paris recounts the Paris Commune of 1871, written by an eyewitness. The author long resisted writing, he confesses. In his excursions he had seen armed bands of every sort. Thousands of individuals of all social positions filled them. So many nationalities mixed there too. He decided compatriots deserved a sincere recital from a disinterested hand. His account aims at that honesty.

The Commune ruled Paris for two months after France's defeat by Prussia. Its fall in Bloody Week killed thousands in the streets. Foreign witnesses wrote many of the surviving narratives. This one stresses the Commune's mixed, improvised character. It is primary testimony from inside a revolutionary city. Read it against official French accounts.
19930-the-boy-ranchers-among-the-indians:
Willard F. Baker wrote The Boy Ranchers series for young readers. Among the Indians takes the boys trailing the Yaquis. Slim, a tall lanky rider on a pony of like build, ambles into view. He tops a slight rise of the trail as Nort laughs. The boys ride a borderland of ranches and raids. Yaqui country lay across the line in Sonora, Mexico.

Boy rancher books taught riding, tracking, and nerve by story. Baker's boys work cattle between adventures. The Yaqui wars were recent and real when he wrote. His fiction softens that history into pursuit and escape. Series readers followed the same crew through many volumes. This one shows the border adventure at full gallop.
20816-socialism-as-it-is:
Roosevelt spoke of a social reordering of the United States, notes Socialism As It Is. A piece in La Follette's Weekly warned against reforms that spare root evils. William English Walling opens his survey of the world-wide revolt with such signs.

Walling, a socialist who knew the movement from inside, maps its parties and plans. Strikes, votes, and revolts across many lands fill his account. He writes for readers who want the facts, not slogans from either side. The book froze a moment in 1912 when socialism seemed poised to reshape the whole industrial world.
20911-the-rose-of-old-st-louis:
A captain stands in a boat's prow, eyeing a village on bluffs past muddy swirls. Mary Dillon opens The Rose of Old St. Louis, from 1904, on that wide river view. Politeness, not true need, prompts the narrator's query on their goal.

French St. Louis, river trade, and old families fill Dillon's historical tale. The rose of the title blooms amid rival claims and young love. Dillon knew the city's French past and wove it with care. Her book keeps a vanished St. Louis alive: Creole manners, keelboats, and a frontier port on the great Mississippi's banks.
21494-trapped-by-malays-a-tale-of-bayone:
George Manville Fenn sets Trapped by Malays in the seas where bayonet meets kris, the wavy Malay blade. A young officer hears laden footsteps pass his quarters at night, then a low call like a night bird. The tale opens in tricks, pranks, and barracks high spirits.

Fenn keeps the action near constant from the first chapters on. Disaster follows disaster, and each escape breeds a fresh trap. The cast recalls his own Middy and the Ensign, with new faces and fresh ground. Readers who love suspense at full stretch will find this a lively, breathless yarn.
22003-the-first-four-books-of-xenophon-s:
Xenophon, an Athenian soldier, marched with ten thousand Greek mercenaries hired by Cyrus the Younger. Cyrus meant to seize the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes. Xenophon later wrote the Anabasis, the classic account of that march. The version here is J. S. Watson's literal English rendering, printed with notes for students in the Handy Literal Translations series.

The first four books cover the long march inland and the start of the retreat. Cyrus falls in battle, the Greek generals are seized by treachery, and the men must fight their way home. They cross harsh mountains in winter with enemies on every side. Generations of schoolboys learned their Greek from these pages.
22023-the-scottish-reformation-its-epoch:
Alexander F. Mitchell, professor of church history at St Andrews, delivered the Baird Lecture for 1899 on the Scottish Reformation. Ill health dogged the work, and the lectures were published after his death in 1900. D. Hay Fleming edited the volume and added a life of the author. Mitchell treats the Reformation by its epochs, episodes, and leaders, as his title promises.

Chapters take up reformers such as Alexander Alesius and Andrew Melville. Long extracts from original sources fill the appendices. Mitchell writes as a church historian who knew the records at first hand. His lectures remain a solid, detailed account of how Scotland broke with Rome and built a Presbyterian church.
22067-the-story-of-a-cannoneer-under-sto:
Edward A. Moore was eighteen and a junior at Washington College in Lexington, Virginia, when the Civil War came. His Story of a Cannoneer under Stonewall Jackson, published in 1907, tells what followed. In the session of 1860 and 1861, he recalls, the students cared more for the coming storm than for their professors. A few classmates were born secessionists; most were decided Union men at first.

Moore joined the Rockbridge Artillery and served with Jackson in the Army of Northern Virginia. He writes of guns, marches, hunger, and the death of Jackson himself. His memoir is valued for its clear, unboastful soldier's eye. Few artillery accounts from the Confederate side read better.
22084-oration-on-the-life-and-character-:
Henry Winter Davis, a Maryland congressman who backed the Union and emancipation, died young in 1865. Congress honoured him with a memorial day in the House of Representatives. The Secretary of the Treasury and other high officers attended. After prayer, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud, and a band played a dirge.

Speaker Schuyler Colfax then introduced the orator of the day. His address traces Davis's life, his fierce speeches, and his stand against slavery's friends in a border state. Such published orations were the official memory of the Civil War generation. This one shows how the House wished Davis, a sharp and lonely figure, to be remembered.
22814-a-practical-guide-to-self-hypnosis:
Melvin Powers published A Practical Guide to Self-Hypnosis in 1961, and his central claim runs through every chapter. All hypnosis, Powers argues, is really self-hypnosis. A person enters the state only when fully ready, and hidden resistance can block the result even when the person insists he wants it at once.

The chapters turn that idea into practice. Readers get steps for relaxing, focusing, and giving themselves suggestions, plus counsel on why early attempts may fail and why practice matters. Powers writes in plain, direct language for lay readers rather than doctors. The guide remains a period piece of the American self-help shelf, and a clear window into how hypnosis was sold to the public then.
22956-rollo-in-paris:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo reaches London on his way to Paris in Rollo in Paris. Hotels there, the narrator explains, generally dine at six or seven o'clock, each family in its own private parlor. One evening near eight, a waiter clears the cloth from the table where Rollo, his parents, and his cousin Jennie have dined.

Abbott built his famous series on travel handled as education. Rollo asks questions, adults answer them well, and a foreign city becomes a lesson in geography, manners, and money. Paris waits across the Channel, with its monuments and its French. Generations of American children toured Europe first through Rollo's eyes. The calm, reasoning tone remains the series' trademark, as distinctive as any adventure.
a-distinguished-provincial-at-paris:
Honoré de Balzac follows Lucien de Rubempré from Angoulême to Paris in Ellen Marriage's translation, the middle part of the Lost Illusions trilogy, as the preparer's note explains. Lucien arrives with a great lady, poems, and hopes of fame. Paris greets him with cold rooms, closed doors, and the price of everything.

Lucien falls in with poor young scholars, then with journalists who teach him to sell his pen and his praise. The theatre, the press, debt, and a love affair with an actress consume his money and his honor. Balzac shows the machinery of literary Paris grinding a gifted young man down, gear by gear.
adventures-and-letters-of-richard-hardin:
Charles Belmont Davis edited this life of his brother, as the title page states. The brother is Richard Harding Davis, the journalist and story writer. The contents run in twenty chapters. They start with the early days in Philadelphia. They pass through college and first newspaper work. They close with the travels that made Davis the most famous American reporter of his age.

Later chapters follow him as a war correspondent. He covered Cuba and Greece. He covered the Spanish-American War and the Boer War. He reported two coronations and the Russo-Japanese War. The end comes with Vera Cruz, the Great War, and his last days. Family letters and the editor's own memories carry the tale between campaigns. The book is both a biography and a record of a reporter's life before radio and wire photos.
anabasis:
Xenophon's Anabasis, in H. G. Dakyns's translation, tells how ten thousand Greek soldiers marched into Persia and fought their way home. The prefatory note gives Xenophon's life in brief: an Athenian, a pupil of Socrates, who marched with the army and helped lead its return between 401 and 399 B.C. The Greeks had hired themselves to Cyrus, who meant to take the throne from his brother.

Cyrus died in battle, the Greek generals were seized, and the army stood stranded deep in a hostile empire. Across seven books Xenophon records marches, snow, hunger, elections of new leaders, and battles on the long road to the sea. Their shout on first seeing the water became famous.
appreciations-of-richard-harding-davis:
Appreciations of Richard Harding Davis gathers memorial essays on the journalist by a dozen of his contemporaries, listed at the front. The writers include Gouverneur Morris, Booth Tarkington, Charles Dana Gibson, Theodore Roosevelt, Irvin S. Cobb, and John Fox, Jr. Each knew Davis as a friend, colleague, or fellow traveler, and each writes in a personal voice rather than a critical one.

Morris opens by remembering games of pirates and imaginary elephant hunts with a man of fifty-two who never grew old. Others recall Davis under fire in Cuba, hunting wounded men in front of the trenches, and the Rough Riders making him an honorary member. Together the pieces form a portrait of the era's model reporter, drawn entirely by the men who shared his world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-diss:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Disentis describes a Benedictine monastery in the Grisons of eastern Switzerland, named for Our Lady of Mercy. Tradition credits Sts. Placid and Sigebert with its foundation in 614, though Mabillon dates it two years earlier.

Avars destroyed the house in 670, martyring its abbot and thirty monks, and Charles Martel with Abbot Pirminius rebuilt it in 711. Charlemagne visited in 800 and heaped benefactions on it, and Abbot Udalric the First became a prince of the empire, a dignity later abbots also held. After a thousand years of independence Disentis joined the new Swiss Congregation in 1617, and St. Charles Borromeo's visit in 1581 crowns its later history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Denis describes the abbey in the town of the same name, four miles north of Paris. Paris' first bishop Denis and his companions, killed in 270, were buried there, and the small chapel over the spot became a famous pilgrimage place in the fifth and sixth centuries.

Dagobert founded a Benedictine abbey there in 630, replacing the chapel with a large basilica, and he and his successors enriched it with gifts and privileges. Possessing St. Denis' shrine, it became one of France's richest and most important abbeys, exempt from episcopal jurisdiction from 653. Charlemagne began a new church in 750, at whose consecration Christ was popularly said to have assisted in person.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abenakis:
The Abenakis were a confederation of Algonquin tribes, including the Penobscots, Passamaquoddies, and Norridgewocks, who once held present-day Maine and southern New Brunswick. Their speech was a dialect of the Micmac tongue, and they sided with the French while resisting English encroachment. When Norridgewock, their chief town, fell and their missionary Rasle was killed in 1724, most of them moved to St. Francis in Quebec.

Remnants survived at St. Francis and Becancourt, on the St. John River, and at Old Town in Maine, with populations the entry counts in the hundreds. The Jesuit Relations describe them as docile, ingenious, temperate in drink, and not profane, and Rasle's dictionary preserved their language. Missions for the remaining people stood at Calais, Eastport, and Old Town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-ecche:
Abraham Ecchelensis was a learned Maronite born at Hekel, or Ecchel, a village on Mount Lebanon, in 1600. He died at Rome in 1664. After study at Rome's Maronite College, he published a Syriac grammar in 1628 and taught both languages at the College of the Propaganda. From 1630 he taught the same languages at the Royal College in Paris and helped edit Le Jay's Polyglot Bible alongside Gabriel Sionita, on Syriac and Arabic texts.

He supplied Third Machabees in Arabic, and Ruth in both Syriac and Arabic, then quarrelled with Sionita. He wrote three letters defending his work against critics, above all Valerian Flavigny. After spells teaching in Rome and Paris, he settled in Rome until his death. His many works include a synopsis of Arab philosophy, a concordance of Eastern Christian nations, and a treatise on the name of pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acta-sanctae-:
Acta Sanctae Sedis is a Roman monthly publication holding the pope's principal public documents, issued directly or through the Roman Congregations. It began in 1865 under the title Acta Sanctae Sedis in compendium redacta, and on 23 May 1904 it was declared an organ of the Holy See.

That declaration gave its contents a special standing: all documents printed in it count as authentic and official. Its monthly rhythm kept clergy and canonists current with Rome's public acts. The short entry thus records a journal that is also a legal instrument, where publication itself confers authority on papal and congregational texts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adeste-fideli:
Adeste Fidelis, a hymn for Benediction at Christmastide, has been used in France and England since the late eighteenth century. London's Portuguese Legation sang it as early as 1797. Vincent Novello, organist there, ascribed the most popular musical setting to John Reading, organist at Winchester Cathedral from 1675 to 1681, then at Winchester College.

St. Bonaventure has been credited with the hymn, but it appears nowhere among his works. French or German authorship is most likely. It calls all the faithful to worship the new-born Saviour at Bethlehem. The entry cites Julian's Dictionary of Hymnology, and its brief notice suits a carol whose words are far more famous than its author.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeterni-patri:
Aeterni Patris is the apostolic letter of Pius IX summoning the Vatican Council, dated at Rome on 29 June 1868. It shares its opening words, and therefore its title, with Leo XIII's scholastic-philosophy encyclical, but their purpose and substance differ greatly. This letter begins by setting out Christ's provision for teaching faith and morals and securing unity in both.

Christ commissioned the apostles to teach, with St. Peter as their head, Prince of the Apostles. That office, for the church's sake, was to live on after Peter's death in a series of successors. Hence Roman pontiffs in Peter's chair inherit the same supreme power, jurisdiction, and primacy. Pontiffs have always guarded faith and morals and, as occasion required, summoned general councils. Pius then summons bishops to a council at St. Peter's on 8 December 1869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alalis: Alalis, also Alalius, was a titular see of Phoenicia, near Palmyra, whose bishops are listed from 325 to 451. Near the Euphrates it stood, a suffragan of Damascus. Its bishop answered to Damascus. The see belonged to Phoenicia, with Palmyra nearby, in the Euphrates region. Lequien's Oriens Christianus, volume two, records the see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-nat:
Alexander Natalis, or Noël Alexandre, was a French Dominican historian and theologian, born at Rouen in January 1639 and dead at Paris in August 1724. He studied at the Dominican College of Rouen, entered the order in May 1655, and took his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1675. Urged by the minister Colbert's circle, he lectured on events of history and then published a complete church history, its first volume appearing at Paris in 1677.

His history ran to twenty-four volumes by 1686, closing with the Council of Trent. Six volumes on the Old Testament followed. Its directness, concision, and critical acumen won praise from Pope Innocent XI and numerous cardinals at first. Later volumes offended Rome by their Gallicanism, and Innocent XI forbade the faithful to read the work in July 1684. In the preface to the third edition of 1699, Father Alexander bowed fully to the Holy See's judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-of-:
Alexander of Lycopolis wrote a brief treatise of twenty-six chapters against the Manichaeans, a dualist sect teaching two eternal powers. He evidently flourished in the early fourth century, since he says he learned the teaching of Manes from one of the man's friends. Despite being brief and at times obscure, the work is prized as a calm, vigorous protest of a trained scientific mind against vague Oriental dogma.

It is asked whether Alexander had been a Christian as he wrote, or ever became one. Photius calls him Bishop of Lycopolis in the Egyptian Thebaid, but Bardenhewer holds he was a pagan and a Platonist. The entry notes a good separate edition by A. Brinkmann, published at Leipzig in 1895, alongside its place in the Greek patrology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexis-paulin:
Alexis Paulin Paris was a French philologist, born at Avenay in Marne in March 1800 and dead in February 1881. After classical studies at Reims, his father sent him to Paris to study law, but he gave his time to literature. In 1824 he published his Defence of the Romantic School, urging imitation of Byron and study of medieval art. He translated Byron's complete works in thirteen volumes, 1827 to 1832.

In 1828 Paris took a clerkship in the King's Library manuscript department, where he pursued medieval literature. He published epics such as Berte aux Grans Piés and Garin le Loherain, and popular songs. He also wrote on Marco Polo and Saint Denis's Great Chronicles. His book on the French manuscripts of the King's Library, published 1836 to 1848, is a dissertation on their authors and contents, not a mere catalogue. He entered the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-lettres in 1837 and helped continue France's Literary History.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alton-illinoi:
The Diocese of Alton covers the Illinois portion south of the northern limits of Adams, Brown, Cass, Menard, Sangamon, Mâcon, Moultrie, Douglas, and Edgar counties. It runs north of the southern limits of Madison, Bond, Fayette, Effingham, Jasper, and Crawford. It was created on 29 July 1853 by dividing the Diocese of Chicago, then covering all Illinois. It was first seated at Quincy and transferred to Alton on 9 January 1857.

Its German Catholic population came largely from Cincinnati, settling at Quincy, Teutopolis, and Germantown, while Swiss Catholics founded Highland and Alsatians Sainte Marie. Henry Damian Juncker, bishop from 1857 to 1868, was born at Fenestrange in German Lorraine in 1809 and died at Alton in 1868. In 1906 the diocese counted 119 diocesan priests, 35 religious, 428 sisters, 143 parishes, and 65 parochial schools with 9,000 pupils.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amastris:
Amastris, now Amasserah or Samastro, is a Paphlagonian titular see in Asia Minor, set on a peninsula jutting into the Black Sea. Gams dates its episcopal list from the third century. Homer mentions it in Iliad book two, it flourished under Trajan from 98 to 117, and it kept some importance until late in the seventh century. The town stood on its peninsula through Roman and early Byzantine centuries alike.

Homer's mention, Trajan's flourishing town, and a see lasting to the seventh century give the small peninsula city a long, thin record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-analysis:
Analysis comes from Greek words meaning to loose or take apart. It names the breaking of a complex thing into simpler parts, the exact counterpart of synthesis, or putting together. A complex thing may be concrete, such as a substance or a process. It may be abstract, such as an idea that exists only in the mind, and each kind is taken apart in its own way.

With a concrete thing, analysis may mean real separation, as when a compound is split into elements, white light into colours, or a machine into pieces. Where parts cannot be cut apart, as in a movement or a thought, the mind still analyzes by varying the groupings and watching what changes. The article closes on ideas themselves, where dropping part of a meaning widens what the idea covers. Child minus under a certain age leaves simply a human being.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anastasiopoli: Anastasiopolis is the name of four ancient episcopal sees, not of one place. They stood in Galatia, as suffragan of Ancyra, in Phrygia, as suffragan of Laodicea, in Caria, and in Thrace. The brief article lists their seats and points to older reference works for more. Readers get a bare identification here, with no history of any single see beyond its province and its superior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipatris: Herod the Great built Antipatris to honour his father Antipater, and Acts 23:31 mentions it. This titular see of Palestine has an episcopal list known from 449 to 451. Smith notes that its ancient name and site still survive today in a Muslim village of considerable size, about three hours' journey north of Jaffa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apocatastasis:
Apocatastasis, Greek for restoration to the original condition, names a doctrine in the history of theology. It holds that a time is coming when all free creatures share in saving grace, including devils and lost souls. It was taught explicitly by Gregory of Nyssa, who compared punishment by fire after death to refining gold in a furnace, separating good metal from dross, or waste. Fire, in this view, is not an end in itself but a cure. Its sharpness and length match the evil in each soul, and it lasts only while evil remains to be burned away.

When all evil ceases, every free will turns to God. The article traces the doctrine through Gregory and later debate, weighing its roots in ideas of purification against church teaching on lasting punishment. Readers get a clear statement of a hopeful but contested hope: that no soul stays lost for ever.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apodosis: Apodosis, a Greek word meaning a giving back, names a usage of the Greek church roughly matching the octave, or eight-day following, of a feast in the Latin rite. Over several days after a great feast the priest turns back to certain prayers of that feast and repeats them in memory of it. The last day of this repetition is called the apodosis. It may run longer or shorter than the Latin week, since great feasts are honoured longer than minor ones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apolysis:
Apolysis, Greek for dismissal, is the closing blessing said by a Greek priest at the end of Mass, Matins, or Vespers. It matches fairly well the Latin Ite, missa est, and has been used in the Greek church since Athanasius's day. At the end of Mass the priest turns to the people. He prays for mercy and salvation through the Mother of God, the cross, angels, John the Baptist, apostles, martyrs, and other saints.

On Sundays the blessing opens with words recalling Christ risen from the dead. On weekdays that opening is left out, since those words mark Sunday as the day of resurrection. A shorter form serves other daytime prayer hours. The entry gives a compact guide to a small rite that closes worship with a wide roll call of heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicae-s:
Apostolicae Servitutis is a bull of Benedict XIV, dated 23 February 1741, against clergy taking up secular business. Despite many church laws against it, some clergy had drifted into worldly trade and pursuits. The bull's object was to check that abuse. It recalled and confirmed statutes of earlier popes and extended them to clergy who tried to dodge penalties by trading under a lay person's name.

It bars clergy from carrying on business begun by lay people unless necessity requires it, and then only with permission. Inside Italy, permission comes from the Sacred Congregation of the Council. Outside Italy, it comes from the diocesan ordinary, or bishop. The entry is a short, sharp statement of a recurring discipline problem. Priests were to live by ministry, not by the market, and the law closed the loopholes they had found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolici-re:
Apostolici Regiminis is a bull of Leo X, dated 19 December 1513, defending Catholic doctrine on the immortality of the soul. It condemned a twofold error then infecting many minds: that the human soul is by nature mortal, and that one single soul animates all people. Others held that doctrine true by natural reason and philosophy, apart from revelation. Leo condemned it in itself and from each point of view.

He appealed to the Council of Vienne in 1311, published by Clement V, which taught that the soul is truly, of itself, and essentially the body's form. From that he declared each soul immortal by nature and each body possessed of its own soul, citing gospel words that killers of the body cannot kill the soul. The entry presents a papal ruling at the meeting point of philosophy and faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicum-p: Apostolicum Pascendi Minis is a bull of Clement XIII, dated 12 January 1765, defending the Society of Jesus against attack. It reports that the Jesuits faced much calumny, or slander, in private and in public, while bishops praised the useful work members did in their dioceses. To confirm that approval and counter the slanders spreading through many countries, the pope confirmed the Society as first constituted. He approved its end, its method of work, and the sodalities, or devout associations, its members directed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apotheosis:
Apotheosis, Greek for deification, means raising people to the rank of gods, and the article traces it from worship of the dead through hero cult to living rulers. Closely tied to universal honour for the dead was the consecration of heroes or rulers as deities, as reward for bravery or great service, and every city worshipped its founder. In the great eastern nations, Persia, Chaldea, and Egypt, the religious character of kingship led peoples to pay divine honours to rulers still living.

Hero worship had taught Greeks that illustrious deeds could make a man a god. Contact with the East made them ready for grosser apotheosis, divine honours offered to the living. Philip of Macedon was honoured as a deity at Amphipolis, and his son Alexander claimed descent from Egyptian gods and decreed his own divinity. The entry follows a practice that blurred the line between king and god.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arcadiopolis: Arcadiopolis was a titular see in Asia Minor, whose bishops' list from 431 to 879 is given in Gams. Gams also lists another see of the same name, with a list over the same years. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus is cited as the source, and the entry does little more than place the see and date its known bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archelais: Archelais was a titular see in Palestine, twelve miles west of the Jordan, whose bishops' list is given in Gams. A second town of that name in Cappadocia was established by Archelaus, last of the Cappadocian kings. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus and Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography are cited, and the entry records little beyond place, distance, and the two towns sharing the name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-areopolis: Areopolis, also called Rabbath-Moab, was a titular see in Palestine, whose bishops' list from 449 to 536 is given in Gams. Another town of the same name stood in Lydia in Asia Minor. Le Quien's Oriens Christianus and Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography are cited, and the entry is a brief gazetteer note distinguishing two places that shared a name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustopolis: Augustopolis was a titular see of Palestine, a suffragan, or subordinate bishopric, of Petra, whose bishops are listed for the years 431 to 536 in Gams. Two other sees bore the same name, and the entry exists to keep them distinct. One stood in Cilicia as a suffragan of Tarsus, and the other stood in Phrygia in Asia Minor as a suffragan of Synnada. That Phrygian list, also in Gams, runs from 359 to 869. No bishop, event, or local history is given beyond these lists and jurisdictions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aureliopolis: Aureliopolis was a titular see, a former bishopric kept on the books in name, in Lydia in Asia Minor. The whole entry is a single line of reference. It points readers to the list of its bishops, covering the years 325 to 787, as printed in Gams on page 447. No bishop, event, or local history is described beyond that pointer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bageis:
Bageis was a titular see of Lydia in Asia Minor, known on coins by that name. Hierocles calls it Bagis, and later lists call it Bage, with the epithet Caesarea. Its coins name the River Hermos, and inscriptions place it near Sirghe on that river. The site is disputed, since the city is said to lie on the north bank while Sirghe stands south.

Harnack's claim that its bishop attended Nicaea is an error, confusing Bageis with Baris, another Lydian city. Gelzer's and Turner's lists stay silent about Bageis, and only three of its bishops are really known. They are Chrysaphius at Ephesus in 431, Leonides in 458, and Basilius in 879. The city still appears in a list of about 1170 to 1179, and it must not be confused with Bagae in Numidia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilinopolis:
Basilinopolis was a titular see of Asia Minor, first a small village in Bithynia Prima. It gained city rank under, or shortly before, Julian the Apostate. Its first known bishop, Alexander, was consecrated by St John Chrysostom about 400. Later bishops include Gerontius in 451, Cyriacus in 518, Sisinnius in 680, Georgius in 787, and Anthimus in 878.

At Chalcedon in 451, Nicomedia and Nicaea fought sharply over its jurisdiction, and the council made it Nicomedia's suffragan. It remained so until about 1170 under Manuel Comnenus. By the fifteenth century it vanishes from episcopal lists, its city doubtless destroyed by the Osmanli. Ramsay places its unknown site west of Lake Nicaea, near Bazar-Keui, between Kios and Nicaea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beauvais:
Beauvais is a suffragan diocese of Reims, re-established in 1822 after the Concordat of 1802 had merged Beauvais, Noyon, and Senlis into Amiens. An 1851 brief lets its bishops style themselves Bishops of Beauvais, Noyon, and Senlis. Tradition credits St Lucianus, martyred about 275 with Maxianus and Julianus, with founding Christianity there. The bishop of 632 to 660 was already the thirteenth incumbent, so the see's exact founding date stays obscure.

Among its bishops are Odo, who answered Photius's grievances with Hincmar, and Gui, founder of St Quentin's great theology school. Pierre Cauchon (1420-32) is tied to Joan of Arc's condemnation, and Cardinal Odet de Châtillon turned Protestant at the Reformation. By the close of 1905 the diocese held 407,808 people, 39 pastorates, and 501 mission parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-guido:
Bernard Guidonis, inquisitor of Toulouse and Bishop of Lodève, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Royères in Limousin in 1261, he died in 1331 after joining the Dominicans at Limoges in 1280. Priorates at Albi, Carcassonne, Castres, and Limoges led to his work as inquisitor against the Albigenses, a heretical movement in southern France.

Pope John XXII rewarded that service with the bishoprics of Tuy and then Lodève. Yet his lasting fame rests on writing: a universal chronicle, lives of saints and popes, and a manual for inquisitors. The entry presents among the Middle Ages' most productive writers, working amid hard duties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardus-pap:
Bernardus Papiensis, an Italian canonist of the thirteenth century, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Pavia, he studied law and theology at Bologna. He served as provost of Pavia cathedral until 1191, then as Bishop of Faenza, and finally as Bishop of Pavia until his death in 1213.

His fame rests on the Breviarium Extravagantium, compiled between 1187 and 1191, gathering ancient canons left out of Gratian's Decretum plus later documents. Later called the First Compilation, it was edited by Friedberg in 1882. A Summa, or summary, on his own book, written while bishop, completes the portrait of a working canonist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-exeg:
Biblical exegesis, the theology of interpreting Scripture's true sense, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The exegete accepts the canon of books on history and Church authority, and takes the Vulgate as the authentic Latin text, without scorning sober textual work on other versions. His task is meaning, not settling the canon or the text.

Senses of Scripture, literal and spiritual, and the rules of the Fathers, from Origen and Augustine to Jerome, fill the survey. A Protestant epigram quoted in the piece, that each reader finds his own creed in the book, warns against private reading unchecked by tradition. The entry is a masterclass in Catholic interpretation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biogenesis-an:
Biogenesis and abiogenesis, rival theories of life's origin, receive a philosophical entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Biogenesis holds that life comes only from earlier life, while abiogenesis holds that life may also spring from lifeless matter. Some thinkers went further, picturing stars and the universe itself as living beings of a higher order.

Careful experiment, the entry says, has proved beyond prudent doubt that visible organisms arise only from germs of their own kind, never from sterile matter. Pasteur's dictum that spontaneous generation is a chimera stands, and Burke's radium cells prove mere gas bubbles. The piece defends biogenesis on experimental grounds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-justi:
Justin de Jacobis, an Italian Lazarist priest, founded the Catholic missions of Abyssinia, now Ethiopia, and led them through prison and exile. Born at San Fele in 1800, he entered the Lazarists at Naples in 1818. He was ordained at Brindisi in 1824. He then served at Oria, Monopoli, Lecce, and Naples before his appointment to Abyssinia.

Named first Prefect Apostolic in 1839, he built missions and schools to train local clergy. In 1847 he received the titular see of Nilopolis, with the vicariate apostolic soon after. He accepted the bishop's office only under pressure in 1849. He died on the road to Halay in 1860 while seeking better health, and his beatification cause opened in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blois:
Blois is the French diocese covering Loir-et-Cher, a suffragan see of Paris with roots in the old Diocese of Chartres. Innocent XII erected it on 1 July 1697. The Concordat of 1802 gave its territory to Orleans, but the diocese was restored in 1822.

Its saints include Solennius, patron of Blois, and monks from Micy and Marmoutier. Among them was Laumer, whose body fugitive monks carried to Blois during the Norman invasions. Peter of Blois defended Thomas Becket in the twelfth century. By late 1905 the diocese counted 275,538 people, 28 pastorates, and 266 mission churches, plus sisters' schools and orphanages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bubastis:
Bubastis, a titular see of Lower Egypt, stands on the Nile's Pelusiac branch near modern Zagazig, and takes its name from the goddess Bastet. Its true name was Bast, or Per-bastet, House of Bastet, rendered in Hebrew as Pi-beseth and in Greek as Boubastis. It flourished under the twenty-third dynasty, about 950 to 750 before Christ, and stood as chief town of the Bubastites district.

When eastern Lower Egypt split into two Augustamnicas, Bubastis fell to the southern one, ruled from Leontopolis, and every district seat held a bishopric. Harpocration appears at Nicaea among Meletius's well-wishers, Hermon held the see about 340, and Julianus attended the Ephesus Latrocinium of 449. In the Middle Ages it merged with Khandek, a Jacobite see near Cairo, sharing bishops like Gabriel in 1078 and John in 1102.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-budweis:
Budweis, a diocese in southern Bohemia suffragan to Prague, was planned from 1630 but erected only under Joseph II by a bull of 20 September 1785. Budweis, Tabor, Prachatitz, and Klattau left Prague's archdiocese to form a see of 5,600 square miles with 660,000 people. Saint Nicholas church became the cathedral, and Prague's archbishop gave 3,300 Rhenish marks toward its endowment.

Its bishops run from Johann Prokop von Schaffgotsche, who served from 1785 to 1813, through Ruzicka, Lindauer, Jirsik, Schonborn, and Riha, to the vicar capitular Hulka in 1907. Three diocesan synods met in 1870, 1872, and 1875. By 1907 the diocese held 1,123,113 people, with 1,106,729 Roman Catholics, about 98 percent, alongside small Evangelical, Jewish, and unaffiliated groups, in Czech, German, and mixed districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-busiris:
Busiris was an Egyptian city mid-Delta, on the Damietta branch of the Nile, whose old name Pa-osiri means House of Osiris. Osiris was held to be buried there, and the name lived on through Coptic Pousiri and Greek forms to Arabic Abusir, the village that stands there now. Busiris headed the Busirite district and became a see of Egypt Secunda.

Its bishop Hermaeon backed Meletius at Nicaea in 325, and later bishops appear at Ephesus in 449 and Chalcedon, where Athanasius apologized for defending Dioscorus. From the seventh century the see figures in Greek patriarchal lists, though its bishops in fact belonged to the Jacobite patriarchate. Later names run from James in 742 through Peter, Severus, and Chail or Michael to Mohna in the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-byllis:
Byllis was a titular see of Epirus Nova in Albania, its title often joined to Apollonia among the suffragans of Dyrrachium. It lay on the coast west of Avlona, near the modern village of Gradica, whose Slav name replaced the old Illyrian Byllis in later episcopal lists. Hierocles knows only Byllis, not the joined title.

Felix, Bishop of Apollonia and Byllis, attended the Ephesus council in 431. At Chalcedon in 451 Eusebius signed simply as Bishop of Apollonia, while Philocharis signed as Bishop of Byllis alone in the bishops of Epirus Nova's 458 letter to Emperor Leo. The see thus appears under both its single and its joined titles in the fifth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesaropolis: Caesaropolis was a titular see of Macedonia whose early name and site still remain unknown. It appears in Gelzer's Nova Tactica and in Parthey's lists of bishoprics as a suffragan of Philippi. Lequien names no bishop, but manuscript notes give two titulars: Meletius, alive in April 1329, and Gabriel, in November 1378.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-callipolis:
Callipolis, now Gallipoli, stands on the Thracian Chersonese where the Dardanelles open. Justinian fortified it and set up great military stores of corn and wine. In 1304 it became the center of the strange rule of the Almugavares, Catalan freebooters who burned it in 1307 before leaving for Cassandria. Turks took it in 1357, their first holding in Europe.

The see depended on Heracleia. Lequien names only six Greek bishops, the first present at Ephesus in 431 and the last about 1500. The Greek see still lives, and rose to a metropolis in 1904. Eight Latin bishops are listed from 1208 to 1518. Today Gallipoli is a district capital of about 30,000 people, Greeks, Turks, Armenians, and Jews, with a Catholic mission run by Assumptionist Fathers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cambysopolis:
Cambysopolis owes its name to a medieval geographer's mistake. After his victory at Issus in 333 B.C., Alexander built Alexandria Minor near Myriandros, a suffragan of Anazarbus. In a tenth-century Antiochene list the name appears jammed into one word, Alexandroukambousou. By the twelfth century that corrupt form was split in two, Alexandrou and Kambysou, creating two episcopal titles for one city.

Lequien names a dozen bishops of the see, among them the martyrs Helenus, Aristion, and Theodore. The Roman Curia today keeps only Cambysopolis, while the true name, Alexandria Scabiosa, survives no more. The city is now Alexandretta, on the bay of the same name, with about 7,000 people, a Catholic parish run by Carmelites, and Sisters of Saint Joseph attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celenderis:
Celenderis, a port and fortress in Isauria, was founded by the Phoenicians or, by legend, by Sandacos, grandson of Phaethon through Astynoös. It appears in the Notitiae episcopatuum down to the twelfth or thirteenth century, listed among the suffragans of Seleuceia. Lequien lists four of its titular bishops, and later writers add more names.

The bishops named include Musonius, who attended in 381, and Julianus, or Julius, present in 451 and 458. Peter sat at the Trullan Council in 692. Eustathius attended Nicaea in 787, with Asterius and Pelagius added from the letters of Severus. Today Celenderis is a small village called Kilindria, with 210 inhabitants, mostly Greeks, and Roman and medieval ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chariopolis:
Chariopolis is a titular see of Thrace about which nothing is known from antiquity. In 1087 it was plundered by the Patzinac and Hungarian kings Tselgou and Solomon, and in 1205 Villehardouin passed through after the failed siege of Adrianople. It appears in later lists of bishoprics under Heracleia in Thrace. An act of Patriarch Isidorus dated 1347 placed it again under Heracleia's jurisdiction.

Lequien names only four of its bishops, the first present at Nicaea in 787 and the last in 1351. When the see ceased to be residential for the Greeks is unknown, though they still use the name for titular bishops. It is now a small town of about 3,000 people northwest of Rodosto, called Khairebolou, Aireboli, or Irebol by the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-franc:
Charles Francois d'Abra de Raconis was a French bishop born at the Château de Raconis in 1580 and dead in 1646. His Calvinist family converted to Catholicism in 1592, and he became an earnest defender of the faith. He taught philosophy at the College of Plessis in 1609 and theology at the College of Navarre in 1615. Three years later he became court preacher and royal almoner, taking an active part in religious polemics and writing works of controversy.

In 1637 he was appointed Bishop of Lavaur, though not consecrated until 1639. Back in Paris in 1643, Jansenist controversies occupied him until his death, with St. Vincent de Paul spurring him on. Two years before he died he published his examination and judgment of the book on frequent communion issued under Arnauld's name. His 1645 work roused his opponents' wrath.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrysopolis:
A short entry on Chrysopolis, a titular see of Roman Arabia, distinct from the Chrysopolis facing Constantinople, now Scutari, which was never a see. This Chrysopolis, suffragan to Bostra in Arabia, appears in neither Hierocles nor George of Cyprus, perhaps because it bore a native name never identified.

The Notitiae Episcopatuum, the lists of sees, name it under the sixth-century Antioch patriarch Anastasius. One Greek bishop only is known: John, present at Chalcedon in 451. Seven Latin titular bishops are known from 1297 to 1648, recorded by Lequien and Eubel. The entry is a brief notice of a small Arabian see kept alive in name long after its city faded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claudiopolis:
Claudiopolis in Bithynia, a titular see of Asia Minor, was the town Strabo calls Bithynium, celebrated for pastures and cheese. Pausanias says Arcadians from Mantinea founded it, and its coins show Claudiopolis as its common name after Claudius. Antinous, Hadrian's favourite, was born there, Hadrian's favourite, whose generosity led to his name joining Claudius's on its coins. Theodosius the Second made it capital of Honorias, a new province formed from Bithynia and Paphlagonia.

Claudiopolis served as religious metropolis of the province in all lists of bishoprics. Lequien names twenty titulars to the thirteenth century, beginning with Saint Autonomus, said to have been martyred under Diocletian, and including Ignatius, friend and correspondent of Photius. The Turks call it Bolou or Boli, chief town of a sanjak with ten thousand inhabitants, on the Filias Sou. No important ruins survive, but fragments of friezes, cornices, funeral stones, and stelae abound.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clovis:
Clovis, also Chlodwig, Childeric's son and king of the Salic Franks, was born in 466 and died at Paris on 27 November 511. He succeeded his father as King of the Franks of Tournai in 481. Though pagan, Childeric had kept friendly relations with the bishops of Gaul. Clovis received a letter from Saint Remigius of Reims. His conquests began against Syagrius, son of Roman count Aegidius.

Established at Soissons, Clovis gained authority over northern Gaul and was called King of Soissons. Syagrius fled to Alaric the Second, who delivered him to Clovis for decapitation in 486. Frankish soldiers plundering a church took a vase the bishop claimed. Clovis sought it to return intact, but a soldier split it with his axe, saying the king would get only his allotted share. The next year, reviewing his army, he found the soldier, reproved his arms, and split his skull, saying: thus you treated the Soissons vase.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregatio-d:
Antonio Astrain's entry treats the Congregatio de Auxiliis, a commission Pope Clement VIII set up to settle the grace controversy between Dominicans and Jesuits late in the sixteenth century. Vast as the dispute ran, its naming question concerned grace's help, auxilia. The crux lay in joining grace's efficacy with human freedom. Efficacious grace, given for an action, infallibly wins man's consent. Yet in acting, man stays free. How can infallible result and liberty harmonize?

Dominicans answered with physical premotion: grace works efficaciously when it premoves the will. The controversy is dated from 1581, when Jesuit Prudencio de Montemayor defended theses attacked by Dominicans. In 1588 Luis de Molina published his Concordia at Lisbon, explaining efficacious grace through middle knowledge, scientia media. Popes sought opinions from Spanish universities and theologians. Clement VIII died on 5 March 1605, and after Leo XI's brief reign, Paul V took the throne with the question still open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantine-l:
Paul Lejay's entry follows Constantine Lascaris, Greek scholar from Constantinople, born 1434, died at Messina in 1501. Prisoner of Turks at Constantinople's fall, he likely spent most of seven years in Corfu. A Rhodes visit won him manuscripts. Reaching Italy, he settled at Milan as a copyist. His work on the eight parts of speech, presented to Princess Hippolyta Sforza, moved her father to ask him to teach her Greek.

He followed her to Naples when she married Alfonso II in 1465. Leaving for Greece the next year, his vessel stopped at Messina, where urging made him stay. He died there after many years, bequeathing seventy-six manuscripts. They stayed at Messina until 1679, then moved to Spain, now in Madrid's National Library. Above all tutor and transcriber, he taught the future Cardinal Bembo. Copyists soon yielded to printing, yet Lascaris wrote the first book printed in Greek, Erotemata, at Milan in 1476.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curubis:
A short entry sketches Curubis, a titular see of Africa Proconsularis. Pompey's generals fortified the town about 46 BC, and Caesar made it a Roman colony named Colonia Julia Curubis. Pliny, Ptolemy, and the Antonine Itinerary all mention it.

In 257 Saint Cyprian was sent into exile at Curubis after refusing sacrifice to the gods, and the next year he was summoned to Carthage for execution. Four bishops are known, one a Donatist, from 411 to 646. Curubis is today Kourba, a small coastal village east of Tunis, in a hilly and wooded region long inhabited by rough peoples, which is why Christians were often exiled there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-darco-antonio:
A biographical entry follows Marco Antonio de Dominis, a Dalmatian ecclesiastic, apostate, and man of science, born on Arbe in 1566 and dead in Sant' Angelo Castle, Rome, in 1624. Schooled at Loreto and Padua, he joined the Jesuits and taught mathematics, logic, and rhetoric. Leaving the order in 1596, he became Bishop of Zengg and Modrus in 1600 and Archbishop of Spalato in 1602.

Siding with Venice against Paul V, quarrelling with clergy and bishops, and losing a financial case at Rome, he resigned and retired to Venice. Threatened by the Inquisition, he fled to England in 1616, welcomed by James I and lodged with Archbishop Abbot. His De Republica Ecclesiastica attacked papal primacy, and his later return to Rome ended in imprisonment. His work on light and rainbows also marks him as a pioneer of optics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-darnis:
A short entry describes Darnis, a metropolitan Libyan titular see in Egypt. Ptolemy and Ammianus Marcellinus place it in Pentapolis, and it became the civil and then religious metropolis of Libya Secunda, or Marmarica. Bishops known number only three, perhaps four, from the fourth or sixth century to around 600.

The city is now Derneh, also written Dernah, Terneh, or Ternah, a small port at the head of a Mediterranean bay where the French admiral Gantheaume came ashore in 1700. It lies east of Benghazi in Tripolitana, with 2,000 inhabitants living by fishing and coastal trade. Darne is another form of the name, while Dardanis is an error, and the entry warns against confusing the two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-de-profundis:
A psalm entry explains De Profundis, Out of the depths, the first words of Psalm 129. Its author is unknown, and it was likely composed during the Babylonian Exile or for Ezra's day of penance. Exile's hard schooling had brought the people to confess guilt and to trust in God's mercy and the promised Redeemer.

The psalm ranks among the fifteen Gradual Psalms sung by pilgrims journeying to Jerusalem, and among the seven Penitential Psalms used early in East and West. In the Divine Office it is sung every Wednesday at Vespers and at second Vespers of Christmas, recalling mercy and plenteous redemption. Above all the Church recites it for the dead, as the psalm of holy souls in purgatory longing for heaven, and at funerals before the body leaves the house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-decapolis:
A geographical entry describes the Decapolis, from Greek for ten cities, a region in Palestine lying south and east of the Galilean Sea. It took its name from the league of ten cities dominating it, and the New Testament mentions it three times, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Josephus, Ptolemy, Strabo, Pliny, and other ancient writers refer to it often.

After Alexander's death, his veterans settled inland, founding or rebuilding Greek cities. Under Seleucids and Ptolemies Greek influence ruled Syria, but Maccabean victories imperilled the towns. In 64-63 BC Pompey made Syria a Roman province and favoured the Greek cities as bulwarks of Roman rule. Only then did the league of the Decapolis form, with rights of coinage and municipal freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocletianopo: This 1913 reference article on Diocletianopolis — the Thracian city, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Balkan hills. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domitiopolis: This 1913 reference article on Domitiopolis — the Isaurian city, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its Christian past. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eduard-heis: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Eduard Heis — the German astronomer. John Hagen honors his famous Atlas. His charts mapped the starry heavens. The observatories prized their learned director. The uranographer of the nineteenth century. His Atlas Coelestis is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-ambros: This 1913 reference piece on Edward Ambrose Burgis — a Dominican of note. Arthur McMahon records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the order's schools. A friar among the historians. His Bibliotheca is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-bellas: A 1913 entry on Edward Bellasis — the herald and antiquary. Herbert Thurston notes his learned works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the College of Arms. A scholar of the Victorian age. His Lancashire pedigrees are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-michel: A 1913 entry on Edward Michelis — a German priest of note. Florence McGahan records his works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the nineteenth century. A writer among the clergy. His Bonn teaching is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eleutheropoli: This 1913 reference piece on Eleutheropolis — the Palestinian city, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiklesis: A 1913 entry on the epiklesis — the Spirit's solemn invocation. Adrian Fortescue unfolds its liturgical place. The priest calls the Hallowing down. The East guards the ancient prayer. The consecration of the Eastern rite. Its Words of Institution frame the rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphanius-of: This 1913 reference piece on Epiphanius of Salamis — the hammer of heretics. Louis Saltet honors his famous Panarion. His pen catalogued the eighty heresies. Cyprus knew its zealous bishop. The detector of the ancient errors. His 374 Panarion is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erzerum-theod: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Erzerum — Theodosiopolis, the Armenian city, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Anatolian highlands. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-esteban-tapis: A 1913 entry on Esteban Tapis — the Franciscan of California. Zephyrin Engelhardt honors his missionary toil. He ruled the missions' golden age. Santa Barbara knew its holy father. The presidente of the California missions. His 1803 presidency is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felice-cavagn: A 1913 entry on Felice Cavagnis — the cardinal canonist. Salvatore Luzio honors his famous Institutiones. His pen ordered the sacred law. The curia prized its learned son. The doctor of the Roman schools. His 1901 red hat is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felicite-robe: A 1913 entry on Lamennais — the Breton prophet. Antoine Dégert unfolds his tragic fall. He dreamed the peoples' free Church. Rome condemned the daring words. The founder of the liberal Catholicism. His 1834 Paroles is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-de-andr: A 1913 entry on Felix de Andreis — the Lazarist of America. John Joseph A'Becket honors his missionary toil. He crossed the seas to the New World. The order prized its pioneer son. The apostle of the western missions. His 1816 voyage is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flaviopolis: This 1913 reference piece on Flaviopolis — the Cilician city, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Taurus foothills. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fractio-panis: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on the fractio panis — the breaking of the bread. Herbert Thurston unfolds its ancient rite. The priest breaks the sacred Host. The faithful share the mystic food. The rite of the Eucharistic banquet. Its Agnus Dei is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-comb: A 1913 entry on François Combefis — the Dominican patrologist. Patrick Healy honors his famous editions. His pen revived the Greek fathers. The order prized its learned son. The editor of the Byzantine texts. His 1679 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-joac: This 1913 reference piece on Bernis — the cardinal-diplomat. Joseph Sollier unfolds his famous career. He served the Pompadour's ministry. The sacred college knew its witty son. The statesman of the Seven Years' war. His 1794 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-rabe: A 1913 entry on Rabelais — the laughing monk of Meudon. Georges Bertrin unfolds his famous Gargantua. His pen mocked the monkish age. The Renaissance laughed at the giant's tale. The Homer of the French humor. His 1553 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-vail: This 1913 reference article on Vaillant de Gueslis — the Jesuit of Canada. Arthur Melançon honors his missionary toil. His zeal served the western missions. The order prized its fearless son. A father among the voyageurs. His 1693 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspard-gusta: A 1913 entry on Coriolis — the French physicist. Henry Brock honors his famous force. His math turned the earthly frame. The Academy prized its learned son. The father of the deflecting force. His 1843 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaston-bruno-: This 1913 reference article on Gaston Paris — the French philologist. Louis Delamarre honors his famous Romania. His pen opened the medieval texts. The Academy prized its learned son. The father of the Romance studies. His 1903 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerardus-odon: This 1913 reference piece on Gerardus Odonis — the Franciscan general. Michael Bihl notes his famous rule. The entry preserves his modest fame. His order served the fourteenth century. A friar among the ministers. His 1342 death is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giraldus-camb: This 1913 reference piece on Giraldus — the Welsh chronicler. James MacCaffrey honors his famous Itinerarium. His pen chronicled the Norman age. The scholars mine his vivid pages. The Bede of the Welsh marches. His 1223 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottschalk-of: This 1913 reference article on Gottschalk — the predestined monk. Michael Ott unfolds his condemned doctrine. He preached the double fate. The synods curbed the daring pen. The heretic of the ninth century. His 868 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gratianopolis: This 1913 reference piece on Gratianopolis — Grenoble, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Alpine hills. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-dub: A 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dubois — the cardinal-regent. Joseph Sollier unfolds his mighty power. He ruled the French kingdom. The Church prized the princely son. The Mazarin's unworthy heir. His 1723 death is famed. His 1721 red hat is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillen-de-ca: This 1913 reference article on Guillén de Castro — the Valencian dramatist. Ventura Fuentes honors his famous Cid. His pen forged the heroic youth. Spain prized the vivid tales. The Corneille's Spanish master. His 1631 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helenopolis: This 1913 reference piece on Helenopolis — the Bithynian city, now a titular see. Sophrone Pétridès notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Propontis shore. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.

catullus-poems-ellis:
Catullus, a Roman poet of the first century BCE, wrote short poems of love, friendship, and attack. Robinson Ellis translated the complete poems and fragments into English. His Lesbia poems remain the most famous part of the set.

Catullus swings between tender devotion and furious insult, sometimes within a page. He pioneered a personal, polished lyric style drawn from Greek models. Poems to his dead brother and to Lesbia's pet sparrow show his range. Some pieces are frankly obscene, and Victorian readers often skipped them. Ellis's notes help students through the dense allusions. Latin poetry rarely feels this immediate or this alive.
cousin-phillis:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Cousin Phillis opens with a lad's pride in his first lodgings. Paul Manning, seventeen, sits in a three-cornered room over a pastry-cook's shop in Eltham. His father, a mechanic with inventive genius, has got him a clerk's place under the engineer building the branch line to Hornby. On Sundays Paul walks to Hope Farm, where his cousin Phillis Holman lives. Phillis is better read than the narrator: Latin, Greek, and Dante are her evening company.

Then Mr. Holdsworth, the engineer, falls ill at the farm and is nursed by Phillis into a love neither declares. He leaves for Canada, and a brain fever does the rest. Readers get Gaskell's most perfect short work here, an idyll where one unspoken sentence carries all the tragedy.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DominicanCrisis:

Together they present the administration's public case for its actions.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_197:

The record thus shows both the pressure for drastic action and a president refusing it, inside a crisis that helped end his presidency and froze two countries into enmity.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:

Belgium's foreign minister said he preferred that allies get twenty-four hours' notice of such plans. The documents show alliance management at the edge of nuclear war: partners informed late, asked to trust decisions that could end their own countries.
jim-davis:
Jim Davis is a boys' adventure novel by John Masefield, published in 1911. Jim tells his own story, starting with his birth in 1800 at Newnham-on-Severn in Gloucestershire. His mother died on the day of the battle of Trafalgar in 1805, and his father four years later. An uncle from Devonshire then took the orphaned boy away from his old home.

The opening chapter lingers on small, sharp memories: masons building a great house, and gypsies camping by the river. It recalls apples from a captain who had killed a man in Spain. Jim's first coach ride scares and thrills him in equal measure. Bacon and eggs at a Bristol inn count as a great treat. These early scenes set up a boyhood that soon turns toward the sea and smuggling.
life-its-true-genesis:
R. W. Wright wrote this 1884 second edition on the origin of life. Catalog metadata credits Horatius Flaccus, but the title page names Wright. His preface opens with Isaiah's call to those who thirst for knowledge. Biblical texts in Hebrew and Greek head the opening pages.

Chapters study seeds, their distribution, vitality, and migration between regions. Wright asks what life is and reviews competing theories. He refutes materialistic theories and judges Darwinism from a vitalist standpoint. The book argues for a spiritual principle behind living things. Forest growth alternations and interglacial periods occupy middle chapters. Isaiah's rain and snow text anchors his law of life.
life-of-john-coleridge-patteson-missiona:

His curacy at Alfington precedes the voyage out in 1855. Chapters track St. John's College, LifU, Mota, and Kohimarama. His episcopate and the Norfolk Island college fill later chapters. The last eighteen months, 1870 to 1871, close the life. St. Barnabas College on Norfolk Island occupies chapter eleven. His fellowship at Merton preceded the Alfington curacy years. Norfolk Island later housed the mission college named for Saint Barnabas.
luther-examined-and-reexamined-a-review-:
Luther Examined and Reexamined reviews Catholic attacks on the Reformer. W. H. T. Dau, a professor at Concordia Seminary in St. Louis, wrote it. Concordia Publishing House issued the book in 1917. Its subtitle adds a plea for revaluation of Luther.

Dau opens with pity for writers tasked with fighting Luther forever. He quotes a Catholic author calling today's problem 'still the Luther problem.' Rome, he argues, cannot admit her moral defeat in the Reformation. Chapter by chapter he answers charges against Luther's life and teaching. The book is a firm Lutheran defense, written for the four-hundredth anniversary year. It shows the old quarrel still alive in 1917.
lysis:
Lysis is a short dialogue by Plato, in Benjamin Jowett's translation. Jowett's introduction notes that it never answers its own question. That question is simple to ask: what is friendship? Socrates puts it to two Athenian boys, Lysis and Menexenus.

The talk unfolds in a wrestling school, amid Greek daily life. Socrates asks whether friends must be alike or unlike. He tests whether friendship springs from need, from goodness, or from desire. Each answer fails, yet the search itself delights. Lysis is a noble, beautiful youth, and Socrates treats him gently. The dialogue is philosophy's first charming look at friendship. It ends in happy puzzlement, as Plato often does.
maha-bharata-the-epic-of-ancient-india-c:
The Maha-bharata, condensed into English verse by Romesh C. Dutt, appeared in 1899. J. M. Dent published it at London in that year. Dutt dedicated his work to the Marquis of Ripon. He thanked Ripon for just rule and self-government in India.

His twelve books follow the great epic's famous arc. A tournament and a bride's choice open the tale. The fatal dice game drives the princes into exile. Then come the falls of Bhishma, Drona, and Karna in battle. Funeral rites and the horse sacrifice close the story. Dutt made India's national epic readable in one volume. His verse is plain, swift, and dignified.
mary-at-the-farm-and-book-of-recipes-com:
